title: Coordination and Response
description: Nervous and hormonal coordination for IGCSE Biology 0610 Core: neurones and the reflex arc, sense organs and the eye, glands and hormones, adrenaline, and an introduction to homeostasis and insulin.

notes.heading: The Nervous System: Impulses and Organisation (14.1.1–3)
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• The nervous system carries information as **electrical impulses** travelling along **neurones** (nerve cells).
• The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the **brain and spinal cord**.
• The **peripheral nervous system (PNS)** is the **nerves outside the CNS**, connecting it to the rest of the body.
• The role of the nervous system is to **coordinate and regulate body functions** — collecting information, processing it and triggering responses.

🔑 What the examiner wants
'Name the parts of the CNS' → brain AND spinal cord — both, not just 'the brain'. 'How is information carried in the nervous system?' → as electrical impulses along neurones; never 'as chemicals in the blood' (that is hormonal control).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Including the sense organs or the skull in the CNS. Receptors and the nerves running to and from them are part of the PNS; only the brain and spinal cord are central.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Electrical impulses travel along neurones.
• CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = the nerves.
• Function: to coordinate and regulate body functions.

notes.heading: Neurone Types and the Reflex Arc (14.1.4–6)
notes.body:
📌 Three neurone types to identify (14.1.4)
• **Sensory neurone** — carries impulses from a **receptor** to the CNS.
• **Relay neurone** — inside the CNS, linking the sensory neurone to the motor neurone.
• **Motor neurone** — carries impulses from the CNS to an **effector** (a muscle or a gland).

📌 The reflex arc (14.1.5) — learn the sequence exactly
**receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector**
A **reflex action** (14.1.6) is an **automatic, rapid** response that integrates a stimulus with the response of a muscle or gland — pulling your hand off a hot object, for example.

🔑 Why reflexes are fast
The impulse travels into the spinal cord and straight back out to the effector; the brain is informed but is not needed to make the decision. Rapid, automatic responses protect the body from harm.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping sensory and motor neurones on a diagram. Follow the direction of the impulse: the sensory neurone runs FROM the receptor TO the spinal cord; the motor neurone runs FROM the cord TO the muscle or gland.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Sensory in, relay in the middle, motor out.
• Reflex = automatic + rapid; effector = muscle or gland.

illustration.alt: A reflex arc showing a receptor in the skin detecting a hot pin, a sensory neurone carrying the impulse to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, and a motor neurone carrying the response to an effector muscle.
illustration.caption: The five components of a reflex arc: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector. The brain is informed afterwards.

notes.heading: The Synapse: the Core Definition Only (14.1.7)
notes.body:
📌 Definition (Core 14.1.7)
A **synapse** is a **junction between two neurones**. That single sentence is the whole Core requirement — learn it word for word.

🔑 Why synapses exist (context, not extra syllabus)
An impulse cannot simply flow from one neurone into the next; the synapse is where the signal is handed over. HOW the handover works — vesicles releasing neurotransmitter molecules that diffuse across a gap and bind to receptor proteins — is a Supplement objective, taught step by step in the homeostasis and coordination extended topic.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing the full Supplement mechanism in a one-mark Core definition question. 'A junction between two neurones' earns the mark; a paragraph about vesicles earns no more and costs time.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Synapse = junction between two neurones.
• The mechanism behind it is Supplement — see the extended topic.

notes.heading: Sense Organs and the Eye (14.2)
notes.body:
📌 Sense organs (14.2.1)
A **sense organ** is a group of **receptor cells** responding to a specific stimulus: **light** (eye), **sound** (ear), **touch** and **temperature** (skin), and **chemicals** (tongue and nose).

📌 Eye structures and their functions (14.2.2–3)
• **Cornea** — the transparent front layer that refracts (bends) light into the eye.
• **Iris** — the coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil.
• **Pupil** — the hole that lets light through to the back of the eye.
• **Lens** — focuses light onto the retina.
• **Retina** — the light-sensitive layer of receptor cells at the back of the eye.
• **Optic nerve** — carries impulses from the retina to the brain.
• **Blind spot** — the point where the optic nerve leaves the eye; there are no receptor cells there, so no image is detected.

🔑 The pupil reflex (14.2.4 — light intensity vs pupil diameter)
Bright light → the pupil **constricts** (gets smaller) → less light enters, protecting the retina. Dim light → the pupil **dilates** (gets larger) → more light enters. It is a reflex: automatic and rapid. The antagonistic iris muscles that drive it are Supplement — see the extended topic.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying the iris 'gets bigger' in dim light. The iris changes shape; it is the PUPIL — the hole — that changes diameter. State the change in pupil diameter and link it to the light intensity.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Sense organs = groups of receptor cells for light, sound, touch, temperature and chemicals.
• Seven eye structures, one function each.
• Pupil reflex: bright → constrict; dim → dilate.

notes.heading: Hormones and Glands (14.3.1–2)
notes.body:
📌 Definition (14.3.1)
A **hormone** is a **chemical substance**, produced by a **gland**, **carried by the blood**, which **alters the activity of one or more specific target organs**. All four elements are needed for full marks.

📌 The glands and hormones to know (14.3.2)
• **Adrenal glands** (sitting on top of the kidneys) → **adrenaline**
• **Pancreas** → **insulin**
• **Testes** → **testosterone**
• **Ovaries** → **oestrogen**

🔑 How a hormone reaches its target
Hormones travel in the blood, so they reach every organ — but only the target organs respond, because only they carry the matching receptors. Glucagon, the second pancreas hormone, is Supplement — see the extended topic.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying hormones are carried 'along nerves' or 'by neurones'. Hormones travel in the BLOOD; neurones carry electrical impulses. Mixing the two systems loses the mark even when the rest of the answer is right.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Gland → hormone → blood → target organ.
• adrenal/adrenaline, pancreas/insulin, testes/testosterone, ovaries/oestrogen.

notes.heading: Adrenaline, and Nervous vs Hormonal Control (14.3.3–4)
notes.body:
📌 Adrenaline in 'fight or flight' (14.3.3)
A threat or sudden stress triggers the adrenal glands to release adrenaline into the blood. The Core effects to quote:
• **increased breathing rate** — more oxygen in, more carbon dioxide out
• **increased heart rate** — faster delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles
• **increased pupil diameter** — more light enters the eye
Together these prepare the body for rapid action.

🔑 Comparing nervous and hormonal control (14.3.4)
• **Nervous** — electrical impulses along neurones: **fast** (fractions of a second) and **short-lived** (the effect stops when the impulses stop).
• **Hormonal** — chemicals carried in the blood: **slower** (the blood must carry the hormone round the body) but **longer-lasting**.
The comparison the exam wants is exactly those two axes: SPEED and DURATION.

💡 Worked Example
'Explain why a reflex, not a hormone, pulls your hand away from a flame.' Nervous impulses reach the arm muscles in a fraction of a second; a hormone would take seconds to arrive via the blood — far too slow to prevent a burn.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Adrenaline: breathing rate ↑, heart rate ↑, pupil diameter ↑.
• Nervous = fast + short-lived; hormonal = slower + longer-lasting.

notes.heading: Homeostasis and Blood Glucose: the Core Start (14.4.1–2)
notes.body:
📌 Definition (14.4.1)
**Homeostasis** is the maintenance of a **constant internal environment** — keeping conditions such as blood glucose concentration and body temperature steady even when the outside environment or the body's activity changes.

📌 Insulin lowers blood glucose (14.4.2)
After a meal rich in carbohydrate, the blood glucose concentration rises. The pancreas releases **insulin**, which causes the blood glucose concentration to **decrease** as glucose is taken up by the liver and other cells. That cause-and-effect — insulin released, glucose falls — is the Core requirement.

🔑 What comes next
The full control loop — glucagon doing the opposite job, the liver converting glucose to glycogen and back, negative feedback, and temperature control through the skin — is Supplement. It is taught in the homeostasis extended topic, which builds directly on these two definitions.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'insulin removes sugar from the blood into the urine'. Insulin acts on body cells, especially the liver; glucose appearing in urine is a symptom of diabetes, not the normal mechanism.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Homeostasis = maintenance of a constant internal environment.
• Insulin decreases the blood glucose concentration.

flashcards.definition: A nerve cell that carries information as an electrical impulse.
flashcards.example: A motor neurone carries impulses from the spinal cord to a muscle.

flashcards.definition: The brain and spinal cord — where impulses are processed and responses coordinated.
flashcards.example: The nerves outside the CNS make up the peripheral nervous system.

flashcards.definition: The pathway of a reflex: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector.
flashcards.example: Touching a hot object triggers the arc that pulls your hand away.

flashcards.definition: An automatic, rapid response that integrates a stimulus with the response of a muscle or gland, without conscious thought.
flashcards.example: The pupil constricting in bright light is a reflex action.
The impulse crosses from the sensory neurone to the relay neurone at a synapse.

flashcards.definition: A group of receptor cells responding to a specific stimulus — light, sound, touch, temperature or chemicals.
flashcards.example: The tongue and nose are sense organs responding to chemicals.

flashcards.definition: The light-sensitive layer of receptor cells at the back of the eye; impulses leave it via the optic nerve.
flashcards.example: The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the retina and there are no receptor cells.

flashcards.definition: The automatic change in pupil diameter with light intensity: pupils constrict in bright light and dilate in dim light.
flashcards.example: Walking into bright sunlight makes your pupils constrict to protect the retina.

flashcards.definition: A chemical substance, produced by a gland and carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs.
flashcards.example: Insulin is made in the pancreas, travels in the blood and acts on the liver.

flashcards.definition: The 'fight or flight' hormone from the adrenal glands: it increases breathing rate, heart rate and pupil diameter.
flashcards.example: A sudden fright releases adrenaline, preparing the body for rapid action.

flashcards.definition: The maintenance of a constant internal environment.
flashcards.example: Keeping blood glucose and body temperature steady are both homeostasis.

flashcards.definition: A hormone secreted by the pancreas that decreases the blood glucose concentration.
flashcards.example: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin release brings the raised blood glucose back down.

questions.stem: The central nervous system is made up of:
choices: The brain only
All the nerves in the body
The spinal cord only
The brain and the spinal cord
questions.explanation: The CNS is the brain AND the spinal cord together — both are needed for the mark. The nerves outside the CNS form the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: In a reflex arc, in which order does an impulse travel?
choices: Effector → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → receptor
Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
Receptor → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → effector
Effector → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → receptor
questions.explanation: The arc runs receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector. The sensory neurone carries the impulse INTO the CNS; the motor neurone carries it OUT to the effector.

choices: The gap between a muscle and the bone it moves
A chemical messenger carried in the blood
A junction between two neurones
The part of the brain that controls reflexes
questions.explanation: At Core, the definition is exactly 'a junction between two neurones'. A chemical carried in the blood is a hormone — a different coordination system.

choices: The adrenal gland
The pancreas
The ovary
The testis
questions.explanation: Adrenaline comes from the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys. The pancreas secretes insulin, the ovaries oestrogen and the testes testosterone.

choices: Pancreas — insulin
Pancreas — testosterone
Ovaries — adrenaline
Testes — oestrogen
questions.explanation: The pancreas secretes insulin. Testosterone comes from the testes, oestrogen from the ovaries and adrenaline from the adrenal glands — the other three pairings each swap two glands.

questions.stem: A reflex action is described as 'automatic'. What does this mean?
choices: It happens only in young people
It is consciously controlled by the brain
It can happen only once and cannot be repeated
It happens without conscious thought — the response is triggered without a decision by the brain
questions.explanation: A reflex integrates the stimulus with a response of a muscle or gland without conscious thought — the impulse travels via the spinal cord and the response begins before you are aware of it. That speed is what protects the body.

questions.stem: Which eye structure focuses light onto the retina?
choices: The iris
The lens
The pupil
The optic nerve
questions.explanation: The lens focuses light onto the retina. The iris controls the pupil's diameter, the pupil is simply the hole that lets light through, and the optic nerve carries impulses away to the brain.

questions.stem: A person steps out of a dark cinema into bright sunlight. What happens in the pupil reflex?
choices: The pupils dilate to let more light in
The pupils stay the same — the reflex only works in the dark
The pupils constrict, reducing the amount of light entering the eye
The cornea becomes opaque to block the light
questions.explanation: Bright light triggers the pupil to constrict, so less light enters and the retina is protected. Dilation is the dim-light response — the opposite direction of change.

questions.stem: The body uses a nerve impulse, not a hormone, to pull your hand away from a flame. Why?
choices: Hormones cannot affect muscles
Nervous effects last longer than hormonal effects
Hormones are only released during sleep
Nervous impulses reach the muscle in a fraction of a second, whereas a hormone carried in the blood would arrive far too slowly
questions.explanation: The nervous/hormonal comparison is speed and duration: nervous control is fast and short-lived, hormonal control slower but longer-lasting. A withdrawal reflex needs speed above all — seconds of delay would mean a burn.

questions.stem: When the image of a small object falls exactly on the blind spot, the object disappears from view. Why?
choices: The blind spot has no receptor cells, so no impulses are sent to the brain from there
The blind spot is covered over by the iris
The lens cannot focus light onto that part of the eye
The blind spot only works in dim light
questions.explanation: The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the retina, so there is no room for receptor cells. Light landing there stimulates no receptors, so no impulses are generated and the brain receives no image.

questions.stem: Minutes after a fright, a person's heart and breathing rates are still raised. What does this show about hormonal control?
choices: Hormones act faster than nerve impulses
Hormones can only affect the heart
Hormonal effects are longer-lasting — adrenaline remains in the blood after the nervous response has ended
The nervous system stops working after a fright
questions.explanation: Hormonal control is slower to start but longer-lasting: adrenaline circulates in the blood and keeps acting on its target organs until it is broken down, which is why the effects outlive the moment of fright.

questions.stem: Which sense organs contain receptor cells that respond to chemicals?
choices: The eye and the ear
The tongue and the nose
The skin and the eye
The ear and the skin
questions.explanation: Taste (tongue) and smell (nose) are the chemical senses. The eye responds to light, the ear to sound, and the skin to touch and temperature.

choices: The maintenance of a constant internal environment
The digestion of food at a constant rate
The growth of the body at a constant rate
The division of cells to replace damaged tissue
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment — keeping conditions such as blood glucose concentration and body temperature steady despite changes outside or in activity.

questions.stem: What is the effect of insulin on the blood?
choices: It increases the blood glucose concentration
It decreases the blood glucose concentration
It has no effect on blood glucose
It increases the oxygen content of the blood
questions.explanation: At Core, the required fact is that insulin decreases the blood glucose concentration — the pancreas releases it when glucose rises after a meal, and glucose is taken up by the liver and other cells.

questions.stem: A student says, 'A hormone only affects organs next to the gland that made it.' Use the definition of a hormone to correct this.
choices: The student is right — hormones diffuse directly to neighbouring organs
Hormones travel along neurones, so they only reach organs connected by nerves
Hormones cannot leave the gland at all
Hormones are carried by the blood all around the body, but only target organs — with the matching receptors — respond
questions.explanation: The definition's 'carried by the blood' element means hormones reach every organ, near or far; the 'specific target organs' element means only organs with the matching receptors respond. Distance from the gland is irrelevant.
